analysis.one_liner: Stops debt collectors from pursuing federal student loan borrowers who owe nothing under income-driven repayment.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House committee vote of 32-24 but was then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee and never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal debt collection law so that a private debt collector working on federal student loans cannot go after a borrower during any period when someone with the same income and family size would owe zero dollars under an income-driven repayment plan. It also caps what a collector can demand each month at the income-driven payment amount, requires collectors to tell borrowers before taking any payment whether they qualify for a discharge of the debt, and limits the government's wage garnishment of defaulted borrowers to people not entitled to discharge and to income-driven payment levels. It cleared a House committee in December 2019 but never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers with low or no income, especially those in default, who would be spared collection calls, demands for money they cannot legally be forced to pay, and wage garnishment above what their income allows.

how_it_helps.text: A debt collector may not attempt to collect a federal student loan debt during any period when a borrower with the same income and family size would owe a zero-dollar payment under an income-driven repayment plan.
A collector may not demand more in any month than the borrower would owe under an income-driven repayment plan.

Before accepting any payment, a collector must certify to the borrower that the borrower is not eligible for any administrative discharge of the debt, so eligible borrowers are told about relief rather than paying a debt that could be wiped out.

The bill limits the Education Department's administrative wage garnishment of defaulted borrowers to people not entitled to loan cancellation, discharge, or forgiveness, and to amounts no greater than an income-driven repayment amount.

analysis.who_pays: Private collection agencies and other contractors paid to collect federal student loans would lose the ability to collect from low-income borrowers and to demand more than the income-driven payment amount, cutting their commissions and fees. To the extent borrowers who owe nothing cannot pay anyway, federal taxpayers would not collect much more under current practice either.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private federal student loan collection contractors

drawbacks.text: The income-driven repayment protections apply only to borrowers whose plans were made on or after July 1, 2014, leaving older borrowers without the same shield.

The bill limits collection but does not move borrowers out of default: a borrower who owes zero dollars could remain in default while interest accrues, and collection agencies argue in good faith that contact with a collector is sometimes how a defaulted borrower first gets enrolled in a repayment plan at all.
Requiring a discharge-eligibility certification before accepting any payment could slow down routine payments for borrowers who want to pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the borrowers it covers, the benefit is real and the cost falls almost entirely on collection contractors rather than taxpayers, since borrowers owed zero dollars under income-driven plans cannot pay much anyway. The design is narrower than a default exit program: it stops aggressive collection of people who owe nothing under the rules without actually cancelling their debts or getting them back into good standing.

outcome.mechanism: It got a favorable 32-24 vote in the House Financial Services Committee, but was then referred to a House Judiciary subcommittee on December 19, 2019 and never came out; it never received a House floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Lawson Jr. of Florida introduced the bill on December 3, 2019, and it was referred to three committees: Financial Services, Judiciary, and Education and Labor.
Only one House Democrat cosponsored the bill.
The House Financial Services Committee held markup sessions on December 10-11, 2019 and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 32-24.
On December 19, 2019 the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, and the record shows no further action.
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 without the House or Senate ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private collection firms on federal student loan contracts kept collecting from low-income defaulted borrowers, including garnishing wages up to statutory limits, and low-income borrowers got no new protection.

sides.party_line_note: The Financial Services Committee's 32-24 vote suggests the bill had majority support but substantial unified opposition in committee, and only 1 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored it; the record does not break the committee vote down by party.

industries.industry: Private debt collection agencies on federal student loan contracts
industries.note: These contractors are paid to collect defaulted federal student loans and earn fees and commissions on what they collect. The bill would bar them from pursuing borrowers who owe zero dollars under income-driven repayment, cap monthly collections at income-driven levels, and force them to tell borrowers about discharge eligibility before taking money, cutting their revenue from the lowest-income borrowers.
